question: How should I position my chair relative to the person with dementia if they are left-handed versus right-handed?
answer: Notice whether the person with dementia is right-handed or left-handed, just as the speaker noticed her preference. If they are right-handed, you can purposely place your chair on their right side. If they are left-handed, you should do it on the other side (their left). This is about their preference and what they like, not your own preference. By sitting on their preferred side, you stay connected with them. You can also sit on the edge of the chair rather than sitting all the way back, which helps you feel more connected and allows you to give gentle touch, like on their knee, if they need that kind of grounding.

question: How can I encourage my loved one to take food themselves rather than having me feed them?
answer: To encourage your loved one to take food themselves, you can try tilting the bowl with one hand while they hold the spoon with the other. This setup can help them open their mouth automatically before the food even arrives, making the process feel more natural. For example, if they are using an underhand grip, you can assist by placing your hands under theirs to support their effort. It is wonderful to see when they manage to take the food themselves, as this shows they are still capable of doing things on their own.

question: How can I tell if my loved one needs help starting to eat or drink?
answer: It can be helpful to watch for signs that your loved one needs a little help just to get started. Sometimes, they need assistance to "initiate" the process, which means helping them begin the action of eating or drinking. This support can act like a trigger for their muscle memory, helping their muscles and brain reconnect so they recognize what is happening. Once you help them start, they may be able to continue on their own.

question: How can I help my loved one use their own hands to hold a spoon and bring food to their mouth?
answer: To help your loved one use their own hands, you can gently tilt the bowl for them while they hold the spoon. Watch for the sign that their mouth is opening automatically before the food even arrives, which shows they are ready. You can assist by placing your hands under theirs to support them as they take the food themselves. It is wonderful to see when they manage to do it on their own, as this builds their confidence.

question: What steps should I take to set up the environment for safe eating assistance?
answer: To set up for safe eating assistance, start by having the person you are helping scoot back just a little bit. This creates space so you can see both of your bodies clearly. Once they are positioned, you can get yourself set up to assist. Remember to take this one step at a time.

question: How does focusing on the person's preferences rather than my own help in caregiving?
answer: Focusing on the person's preferences rather than your own helps you connect with them and support their specific needs. For example, if you notice the person is right-handed but you are left-handed, you should place your chair on the right side to match their preference. This approach allows you to build skills, such as helping them use their non-dominant hand if it supports them better, instead of relying on your own habits. It also helps you notice their physical positioning, like sitting on the edge of the chair, so you can offer grounding touch, such as proprioceptive touch on their knee, if they need it. Ultimately, it is about their likes, not yours.

question: What happens if the caregiver sits in a different position while feeding?
answer: If a caregiver sits in a different position, the food might come from the side instead of the center. This feels unnatural for the person being fed and can lead to a difficult or "bad" bath experience. To prevent this, the caregiver should sit so the cup is right in front of the person, ensuring the food travels up the center line of their body.

question: How do I know if my loved one will always need help with every meal?
answer: Based on the video, you cannot know for sure if your loved one will always need help with every meal, as needs can vary from person to person. For example, one person might need assistance now, while another might only need help to start eating. A helpful strategy is to use "hand-under-hand" assistance, where you gently guide their hand to help them initiate the action. This can trigger their muscle memory and help their brain reconnect, allowing them to continue eating or drinking on their own once they get started.

question: How can I demonstrate the hand position needed for the person to pick up a spoon?
answer: To help the person pick up a spoon, you can use a specific hand position that supports their arm. First, place your hand under their shoulder instead of letting it rest there. Next, position their elbow in the crook of your elbow. Finally, use your skill fingers (which means your fingers that are ready to help or guide) to assist them. This setup makes the task a bit trickier but provides the right support for eating.

question: Why is it helpful to place my hand on my loved one's shoulder while holding their hand?
answer: Placing your hand on your loved one's shoulder while holding their hand is helpful because it gives them a little pressure that lets them know you are there. This type of touch, which the video calls "proprioceptive touch" (a feeling that helps the brain understand where your body parts are in space), also helps remind their brain to connect the sensation from your shoulder to your hand. To do this, you can put your hand on their shoulder while keeping your fingers interlocked with theirs, using your fingers to stay connected and giving a gentle, nice pressure.

question: How does sitting on the center line of the body help with feeding?
answer: Sitting on the center line of the person's body helps because it makes the food feel natural and easy to reach. If you sit to the side, the food comes from the side, which can feel unnatural and might cause the person to get a "bad bath" (meaning they might spill or struggle to eat). To do this correctly, place the cup right in front of them so it is directly in the center line of their body. This position ensures the food comes from the front, which is the most comfortable way for them to eat.

question: What is the correct way to place the bowl so the person can reach it with their hand?
answer: To help the person reach the bowl, place it near their shoulder instead of on their shoulder. Then, position their elbow in the crook of your elbow. This setup allows you to use your skill fingers to assist them with eating.

question: Why is it important to have my back leg positioned behind the chair?
answer: Having your back leg positioned behind the chair helps you stay spread out, which allows you to reach and connect with the person you are caring for more easily. This setup lets you have your cup and bowl ready without needing to move around or bring items over while you are interacting with them. By getting your general position (PPA) set up this way, you can focus on being connected rather than trying to manage your belongings at the same time.

question: What is the best way to position a bowl to help someone with dementia eat more independently?
answer: To help someone with dementia eat more independently, you can tilt the bowl using the hand that is not holding the spoon. This position helps ensure their mouth is open before the food arrives, which can make eating feel automatic. You can also try letting them take the food themselves, perhaps with your hands positioned underneath to assist if needed. It is okay if they need a little help; the goal is to support them in doing as much as they can on their own.

question: How should I hold my loved one's hand to help them feel connected?
answer: To help your loved one feel connected, gently place your hand over theirs so your fingers are interlaced with theirs. You can use your fingers to stay connected and even give a little bit of nice pressure. To let them know you are there, you can also place your hand on their shoulder to give a little pressure. This type of touch, called proprioceptive touch, helps remind their brain that you are present and helps them feel the connection from one part of their body to another.

question: How should I hold a cup to help someone with dementia use their skilled fingers instead of bending their wrist?
answer: To help someone use their skilled fingers instead of bending their wrist, hold the cup like you would normally, but adjust your grip so their hand is positioned under the cup. This allows them to use their skilled fingers to help move the cup up the center line. This method is helpful because it lets them give you feedback on whether they are done or if they are really thirsty, rather than having to bend their wrist to get the cup back.

question: How should I position myself and the person with dementia before helping them eat?
answer: Before helping someone with dementia eat, it is important to set up the space so you can see each other's bodies clearly. First, ask the person to scoot back just a little bit in their chair. This creates enough space for you to get yourself set up comfortably beside them. By doing this step by step, you ensure you are both positioned correctly to assist safely.

question: How does spreading my body out help me connect with the person with dementia?
answer: Spreading your body out helps you get closer to the person with dementia, which makes it easier to connect. In the video, the educator shows that by sitting with your back leg behind the chair and spreading out, you can place your cup and bowl right in front of you. This setup means you don't have to reach over or bring items from far away while trying to connect. Instead, you can use your "general PPA" (a general approach or method mentioned in the video) to stay connected because everything is already set and ready to go.
